title: Journal entries in practice: from the rule to the ledger
subtitle: Debits and credits for the transactions you meet every day, and a startup's first month
openingQuestion: You sell 200m of goods and the customer will pay next month. Which entry do you book?
openingOptions: Nothing yet - wait for the cash before recognising revenue
explanation: Revenue is recognised when the obligation is fulfilled, not when the cash arrives - that is the accrual principle. The goods have been delivered, so the revenue arises immediately, and because no cash has come in, the other side is a receivable rather than cash. A receivable is an asset, and an asset increasing is a debit; revenue increasing is a credit. Swapping the two sides says revenue fell and receivables fell too, which describes a completely different transaction. Booking it to cash is wrong in a different way: the ledger would report 200m sitting in the bank when not a single dong has arrived.

diagram.label: Classify: asset, liability, equity, revenue or expense
Apply the increase/decrease rule to each type
Debit first, credit second, both sides equal

realWorldExample.description: The first four transactions of a new company touch all four account types: shareholders putting in capital, rent paid in advance, buying equipment, and selling a service with half the cash collected. Read those four entries and you can read most of a small company's ledger.

keyTakeaways: Three steps: identify the accounts, classify them, then apply the increase/decrease rule
Revenue is booked when the obligation is met, not when the cash arrives
Spending cash on an asset creates no expense - it only changes the form of wealth
Depreciation is a non-cash expense: debit the expense, credit accumulated depreciation

summary.keyIdea: Every transaction is one question: which account did the value move from, and to which
summary.commonMistake: Recognising revenue when the cash lands, and treating every payment out as an expense
summary.action: Take the five most recent transactions of a business you know and write both sides of each yourself

application.title: Keep a month of books yourself
application.message: Take one month of your own spending, treat yourself as a one-person company, and write both sides of every item. Wherever you find it hard to classify is usually the boundary between an asset and an expense.
application.secondary: If the two sides don't balance, the error is almost always a transaction where you only booked one side.

practicePrompt.question: A company pays 120m in advance for six months of office rent. What is the entry at the moment of payment?
practicePrompt.explanation: At the moment of payment the company has not occupied anything yet - it has bought the right to use the office for the next six months, and that right is an asset. So the debit is a prepayment, not an expense. The expense arises gradually: each month 20m moves from prepayments into rent expense. Booking the whole 120m as an expense at once crams six months into one, making that month's profit falsely low and the next five falsely high. The last option doesn't even balance.

sections.text: The debit-credit rule is short, but the difficulty is not in the rule: it is in recognising which accounts a transaction actually touches. This part walks through the transactions you meet every day, and through the first month of a new company.

sections.label: The groundwork is in the previous lesson
sections.text: Why every transaction has two sides, the increase/decrease rule for each account type, and why the total always balances - all of that is in the double-entry lesson. Here we only apply it to real work.

items: Identify the accounts affected: cash, inventory, revenue, a loan, and so on
Classify each one as an asset, a liability, equity, revenue or an expense
Apply the increase/decrease rule, write the debit first and the credit second, then check the two sides are equal
Buying an asset for 500m cash: debit fixed assets, credit cash - two assets swap places and total assets are unchanged
Selling 200m of goods on credit: debit receivables, credit revenue - the revenue is booked even though no cash has arrived
Collecting the 200m from the customer: debit cash, credit receivables - a conversion between two assets, with no new revenue
Depreciation of 50m: debit depreciation expense, credit accumulated depreciation - an expense arises without a single dong leaving

sections.text: The middle two are where people slip most often, because the same 200m figure appears twice. The first time it creates revenue, the second time it does not - and booking revenue on both occasions makes the ledger report twice the revenue that actually exists.

items: Shareholders contribute 2bn: debit cash 2bn, credit share capital 2bn
Six months of rent paid in advance, 120m: debit prepayments 120, credit cash 120
Buying a laptop for 50m: debit equipment 50, credit cash 50
Selling 300m of services with half collected immediately: debit cash 150 and debit receivables 150, credit revenue 300

sections.text: The last transaction shows that one credit can be matched by two debits. What has to balance is the total of the two sides, not the number of lines: 150 plus 150 is 300.

lines: The ledger can detect its own errors because total debits must equal total credits, so an imbalance almost always means a transaction was booked on one side only.
But balancing does not mean correct: post the right amount to the wrong account and the ledger still balances.

quiz.question: You buy 200m of inventory and pay cash. Which entry is correct?
quiz.explanation: Inventory (an asset) rises → debit inventory. Cash (an asset) falls → credit cash. This is an exchange between two assets.

quiz.question: The company borrows 500m from a bank and the money lands in its account. What is the entry?
quiz.explanation: Cash (an asset) rises → debit cash. Loan payable (a liability) rises → credit loan payable. Debt and assets go up together.

quiz.question: You pay 100m of staff salaries in cash. What is the entry?
quiz.explanation: Salary expense (an expense) rises → debit it. Cash (an asset) falls → credit cash. The expense reduces profit, and so reduces equity.

quiz.question: A customer pays a 50m deposit and nothing has been delivered yet. What is the entry?
quiz.explanation: Nothing delivered means nothing earned. Book deferred revenue (a liability) - the obligation to deliver later. Only on delivery do you post Dr. Deferred Revenue / Cr. Revenue.

quiz.question: After the year-end close, what happens to the revenue and expense accounts?
options: Their balances carry forward into the following year
Their balances are transferred straight onto the balance sheet
They go to zero, with the profit or loss moved into retained earnings
They are deleted entirely from the accounting system
quiz.explanation: The closing entries are Dr. Revenue / Cr. Income Summary, then Dr. Income Summary / Cr. Retained Earnings if there is a profit. Revenue and expense are temporary accounts and reset every year.
